column4: Adopt recognised certifications for key categories
column5: Introduce certification to demonstrate responsible sourcing and deforestation avoidance
column6: MSC / ASC Chain of Custody and certification guidance – useful for seafood because it helps members understand certification requirements, supply-chain traceability and how certified products can be verified through procurement. Fairtrade / Organic certification guidance can be used in the same way for relevant commodities.
column9: Establish category-specific requirements to purchase food and beverage products through recognised environmental, ethical or responsible-sourcing certification schemes. Prioritise categories with significant environmental, social or traceability risks and periodically verify supplier compliance.
column10: Improves sourcing transparency and traceability, provides independently verified minimum standards, reduces environmental and reputational risks, and supports credible customer-facing claims.
column11: Identify the food and beverage categories with the highest sourcing, traceability or sustainability risks and select appropriate recognised certification schemes for each category. Incorporate certification requirements into procurement specifications and supplier contracts, request valid certification or chain-of-custody evidence from suppliers, and periodically review the percentage of relevant spend or volume covered.
column12: Percentage of spend in priority food and beverage categories covered by recognised certification schemes
column13: Whitbread / Premier Inn: Premier Inn became the world’s largest MSC-certified hotel chain, with 635 locations certified and an additional 3 million portions of certified sustainable fish and chips expected to be served across the UK.
column15: Variable. Certification may involve application, audit, inspection and annual licence fees. Costs vary materially by scheme, organisation size and supply-chain complexity.
column16: Not directly quantifiable as a generic tCO2e saving. Certification primarily provides traceability and assurance; actual carbon impact depends on the commodity, production system and sourcing change achieved.
column17: Typically months rather than years for initial certification, depending on existing traceability systems and audit readiness. No universal ROI.
column18: % of priority-category spend certified; certified product/volume share; number of categories covered; supplier compliance rate.

column4: Set targets to increase local/regional and seasonal sourcing to reduce transport emissions and support UK producers
column6: UK Government GHG Conversion Factors – useful when members have real transport-mode, weight and distance data and want to compare transport emissions between sourcing options. Seasonality calendars / supplier origin data – useful for identifying when UK or regional produce is actually in season before changing procurement specifications.
column9: Set measurable sourcing targets for seasonal, local or regional ingredients where these options offer credible environmental, quality, traceability or resilience benefits. Decisions should consider production methods and transport modes rather than assuming that local sourcing is always lower carbon.
column10: Can strengthen supply-chain resilience, improve freshness and traceability, support regional suppliers and reduce exposure to seasonal or transport-related disruption when sourcing decisions are based on full environmental impacts rather than distance alone.
column11: Map the origin, seasonality and transport mode of major produce categories. Identify products where seasonal or regional sourcing can genuinely improve resilience or reduce high-impact transport, particularly air freight. Set measurable sourcing targets, work with suppliers to identify suitable alternatives, and review performance by spend, volume and transport mode rather than assuming that all local products are automatically lower carbon.
column12: Percentage of relevant food and beverage spend sourced locally, regionally or seasonally against the defined target
column13: Greene King: Working with Fresh Direct, Greene King committed to removing airfreighted fresh fruit and vegetables from menus across 1,600 managed pubs from Autumn/Winter 2025. Its fresh-produce purchasing exceeds 9 million kg annually.
column15: No verified aggregate saving publicly disclosed. Cost effects depend on season, commodity, supplier and transport mode. Seasonal sourcing may reduce exposure to expensive air freight, but local sourcing is not inherently cheaper.
column16: Potentially positive, especially when air freight is avoided. Carbon impact should be assessed using production method and transport mode rather than distance alone.
column17: Menu/supplier changes can potentially be implemented within one or several menu cycles. No generic ROI is available because procurement prices vary by ingredient and season.
column18: % relevant spend/volume seasonal or regional; % fresh produce transported by air; food miles where meaningful; kgCO₂e/kg purchased.

column4: Pilot new sourcing models with innovative/smaller suppliers to diversify supply and de-risk from commodity volatility
column6: Supplier pilot scorecard / procurement assessment template – useful because members need to compare new suppliers consistently across price, quality, sustainability, resilience and operational performance rather than evaluating only purchase price. Foodbuy Pitch Social can be used as a practical peer example of how large foodservice buyers can identify and support smaller or purpose-led suppliers, but it is more a programme example than a universal tool.
column9: Trial alternative sourcing arrangements with smaller producers, cooperatives, farmer groups or direct-trade partners. Assess whether these models improve traceability, supply resilience, producer relationships, sustainability performance and exposure to commodity-price volatility before scaling them.
column10: Diversifies the supplier base, improves traceability and producer relationships, creates opportunities for innovation, and can reduce dependency on concentrated commodity markets or individual suppliers.
column11: Identify categories where the business is overly dependent on a small number of suppliers, where commodity-price volatility is material or where traceability is weak. Select a small number of alternative suppliers, farmer groups or direct-trade partners for controlled pilots. Compare product quality, total delivered cost, logistics, traceability, sustainability performance and supply reliability before deciding whether to scale the relationship.
column12: Number of innovative sourcing pilots completed and percentage progressing to scaled or longer-term supply arrangements
column13: Foodbuy Group: Its Pitch Social programme gives SMEs and purpose-led suppliers access to its foodservice procurement network. The 2026 event involved 18 suppliers and 100+ attendees, while Foodbuy reported cumulative spend with social enterprises had reached £25 million.
column15: Pilot-dependent. Small pilots can be run within existing procurement budgets, although onboarding, assurance and logistics can add costs. No transferable saving is publicly disclosed.
column16: Not inherently a carbon-abatement initiative. Carbon benefits only arise where the new sourcing model demonstrably reduces production, logistics or other lifecycle emissions.
column17: A pilot could normally be assessed over one or more procurement/menu cycles. No standard ROI; scale only after commercial and sustainability performance has been demonstrated.
column18: # pilots completed; % converted to long-term contracts; £ spend with SMEs/innovative suppliers; supplier concentration; traceability/data coverage.

column4: Proportion of plant-based dishes on the menu
column5: Increase proportion of plant-based dishes on the menu
column6: Foodsteps or another food carbon-footprinting platform – useful because it allows members to compare the carbon footprint of plant-based and conventional dishes at recipe or serving level rather than assuming that every plant-based option has the same impact. Menu sales/POS data should be used alongside it to check whether increased availability actually changes customer purchasing.
column9: Establish a baseline and measurable target for increasing the availability and variety of plant-based dishes. Integrate suitable options across menu categories while maintaining nutritional quality, customer appeal and commercial performance.
column10: Reduces exposure to emissions-intensive animal proteins, broadens customer choice and can lower the overall carbon footprint of the menu while responding to growing demand for plant-rich options.
column11: Establish the current share of plant-based dishes and their sales as a baseline. Set a realistic target for increasing plant-based availability across relevant menu categories, develop and test dishes for taste, nutrition, cost and customer appeal, and train kitchen and front-of-house teams where required. Track both menu availability and actual sales so that options that perform well can be retained and scaled.
column12: Plant-based dishes as a percentage of total customer-facing menu items
column13: Levy UK & Ireland: Levy reports that 86% of dessert items are plant-based, with more than 60% of venues offering fully plant-based dessert menus. Procurement mass of plant-based milk and cream increased 414% between FY2019 and FY2024.
column15: Potential cost saving, but recipe-specific. Financial performance depends on ingredient mix, recipe design, sales and customer uptake; no universal hospitality-wide £ saving should be applied.
column16: High potential where plant-rich dishes displace emissions-intensive animal proteins. Actual savings should be calculated recipe-by-recipe using consistent lifecycle boundaries.
column17: Menu changes can be introduced within normal menu-development cycles. Financial payback can be immediate where ingredient costs fall, but there is no universal ROI.
column18: % menu items plant-based; plant-based sales share; kgCO₂e/meal; plant-based procurement volume; customer acceptance.

column4: Procure items sourced from ingredients grown using regenerative practices
column5: Introduce menu items sourced from ingredients grown using regenerative practices
column6: Supplier farm-practice evidence / regenerative sourcing frameworks – useful because “regenerative” does not currently have one universally applied definition, so members need documented criteria and supplier evidence before making claims. Product carbon footprint or LCA tools, where available, can help compare the environmental performance of regenerative and conventional alternatives on a consistent basis.
column9: Develop and introduce menu items containing ingredients produced through regenerative or other credible nature-positive agricultural practices. Define acceptable sourcing criteria and obtain sufficient supplier evidence to support related claims.
column10: Supports farming practices intended to improve soil health, biodiversity and ecosystem resilience, while helping businesses build more resilient ingredient supply chains and credible nature-positive menu propositions.
column11: Identify agricultural ingredients where regenerative sourcing is commercially and operationally feasible. Define minimum evidence requirements for what the business will accept as regenerative or nature-positive sourcing, engage suppliers that can demonstrate relevant farming practices and provenance, and begin with a limited number of ingredients or menu items. Review cost, availability, supplier evidence and measurable nature or carbon outcomes before scaling.
column12: Percentage of relevant agricultural ingredient spend or volume sourced under verified regenerative or nature-positive criteria
column13: Shake Shack UK: Shake Shack introduced Wildfarmed regenerative flour into potato buns across all UK locations. After one year it reported using 35 tonnes of regenerative flour, with 25% regenerative flour in every potato bun.
column15: No price premium or cost saving publicly disclosed by Shake Shack. Costs depend on commodity, contract scale, verification requirements and supplier availability.
column16: Carbon benefit is plausible but not quantified by Shake Shack. The company does not publish a verified tCO2e saving for the bun sourcing change.
column17: Procurement substitution could be implemented within a supplier-contract or menu cycle, subject to supply availability and product testing. ROI is not publicly disclosed.
column18: % relevant spend/volume regenerative; tonnes sourced; % recipes/products converted; supplier verification coverage; kgCO₂e/kg where verified farm data exist.

column4: Design the menu to highlight and nudge customers toward lower-carbon choices
column5: Design your menu to promote, highlight and encourage low carbon choices
column6: WRI food-service behavioural guidance / menu-design resources – useful because WRI provides evidence-based approaches to naming, positioning and promoting plant-rich dishes rather than relying on intuition. A/B testing using POS or digital-menu data is useful for determining whether the intervention actually changes sales in the member’s own customer base.
column9: Use menu layout, product placement, descriptions, defaults, naming and promotional techniques to make lower-carbon options more visible, attractive and convenient. Test customer response and avoid misleading environmental claims.
column10: Increases the visibility and attractiveness of lower-carbon dishes, influences customer choices without removing freedom of choice, and can increase sales of plant-rich meals.
column11: Identify dishes that are lower carbon and commercially suitable for promotion. Test behavioural interventions such as menu placement, naming, descriptions, defaults, imagery or promotional positioning. Compare sales against a baseline or control group and retain interventions that increase uptake without negatively affecting customer satisfaction, margin or credibility of environmental claims.
column12: Percentage of lower-carbon dishes receiving menu-design interventions and change in their sales share
column13: WRI UK food-service research: Changing the description of “Chickpea and Potato Curry” to “Mild and Sweet Chickpea and Potato Curry” increased stated ordering by 108%. WRI also cites research where flavour-focused descriptions increased selection by 41% compared with health-focused labels.
column15: Very low implementation cost where changes are limited to digital menus, naming, positioning or menu design. Printing or re-platforming costs may apply. No universal £ saving.
column16: Indirect but potentially material. Carbon savings depend on the number of customers switching and the carbon-footprint difference between the promoted dish and displaced alternative.
column17: Can be tested within weeks or one menu cycle. Potentially rapid commercial return because the intervention can require little or no capex.
column18: Change in lower-carbon dish sales share; conversion/uplift vs baseline; kgCO₂e per transaction/meal; gross margin; customer satisfaction.

column4: Swap high-impact ingredients for lower-impact equivalents where they don't compromise the dish
column6: Foodsteps or another recipe-level carbon-footprinting tool – useful because it can quantify the before-and-after carbon impact of recipe reformulation at serving level. Recipe-costing tools are also important because members need to assess carbon reduction alongside ingredient cost and margin, not carbon alone.
column9: Review high-impact ingredients and trial lower-impact substitutes, such as blended meat products, reduced dairy or cream content and alternative proteins. Assess carbon impact, nutrition, allergens, cost, taste and customer acceptance before wider implementation.
column10: Reduces the carbon and resource intensity of dishes, can lower ingredient costs and supply-chain exposure, and enables emissions reductions while retaining familiar menu formats.
column11: Use recipe-level carbon and cost information to identify ingredients responsible for a large share of a dish's footprint. Develop lower-impact substitutes such as blended meat products, lower dairy content or alternative proteins, then test them for carbon impact, ingredient cost, nutrition, allergens, taste and customer acceptance. Standardise successful recipes and update procurement specifications before wider rollout.
column12: Percentage of priority recipes reformulated with verified reductions in ingredient-related carbon impact
column13: Levy: Levy introduced its 50:50 beef-and-mushroom burger. Between FY2019 and FY2024, emissions associated with its beef-burger portfolio fell 71.5%. Levy also reports a plant-based panna cotta at QEII Centre producing 43% less CO2e per serving than its dairy version.
column15: Recipe-specific. Ingredient substitution can reduce food cost where expensive animal proteins are partly replaced, but Levy does not publish a transferable £ saving per burger/dish.
column16: Strong and directly measurable at recipe level. Levy reports 43% lower CO2e per serving for the plant-based panna cotta. The 71.5% beef-burger portfolio reduction should not be attributed solely to the blended burger.
column17: Recipe trials can generally be completed over weeks/months and a menu cycle. Usually little/no capex; ROI depends mainly on ingredient cost and customer uptake.
column18: % priority recipes reformulated; kgCO₂e/portion before vs after; % carbon reduction/recipe; ingredient cost/portion; sales/customer acceptance.

column4: Use nose-to-tail cooking to reduce waste from higher-impact proteins
column6: Winnow or another food-waste measurement system – useful because members first need to know where and how much protein is being wasted before redesigning butchery or recipes. Butchery yield / trimming logs are also useful because they isolate animal-protein utilisation more precisely than total kitchen-waste data.
column9: Where animal products remain on the menu, develop recipes and kitchen practices that use a wider range of edible cuts and by-products. Ensure appropriate staff skills, food-safety controls, customer acceptance and demand planning so that the initiative does not create additional waste.
column10: Improves utilisation of purchased animal products, reduces avoidable preparation waste and purchasing losses, and can create additional menu value from underused cuts where food-safety and demand controls are effective.
column11: Measure current animal-protein trimming and preparation waste to identify edible material that is currently being discarded. Develop recipes that safely use appropriate secondary cuts, trimmings or by-products, train kitchen teams in preparation techniques and food-safety requirements, and track edible yield and waste after implementation. Ensure new dishes are supported by actual demand so that reuse does not simply create another form of waste.
column12: Percentage of applicable animal-protein purchases utilised through nose-to-tail menu applications, or reduction in preparation waste from animal proteins
column13: MGM COTAI: Using food-waste data and improved butchery practices, MGM achieved a 66% reduction in butchery trimming waste by weight. Its kitchens also repurpose edible animal-protein offcuts.
column15: Potential food-cost saving through higher utilisation of purchased proteins. No separate saving attributable solely to butchery optimisation is disclosed.
column16: Carbon benefit comes from avoiding wasted high-impact proteins and reducing replacement purchasing. The wider MGM programme has carbon benefits, but these cannot be attributed solely to nose-to-tail practices.
column17: Operational changes can potentially be introduced over weeks to months after measurement, recipe development and staff training. Usually low capex; return comes from avoided food purchases.
column18: kg animal-protein waste / kg purchased; edible yield/utilisation %; trimming waste reduction %; £ waste avoided; kgCO₂e avoided.

column4: Adjust portion sizes and prep quantities based on waste data
column5: Optimise portion sizes to reduce plate waste
column6: Winnow or another food-waste smart-scale system – useful because it provides dish-level and production-level waste data that can identify exactly where portioning and preparation are creating waste. Sales/POS and covers data should be combined with waste data so preparation quantities can be linked to actual demand rather than adjusted in isolation.
column9: Use sales, covers, plate-waste and production-waste data to adjust serving sizes, batch preparation and purchasing quantities. Review results regularly to reduce overproduction and plate waste without negatively affecting customer satisfaction or nutritional requirements.
column10: Reduces overproduction, preparation waste and plate waste, improves demand forecasting and purchasing efficiency, and can deliver both cost savings and emissions reductions.
column11: Measure plate waste, preparation waste, sales and covers by dish and service period. Use the data to identify oversized portions, overproduction and inaccurate demand assumptions. Adjust portion specifications, purchasing quantities and batch-preparation levels, using smaller or more frequent production batches where appropriate. Continue monitoring food waste per cover and customer satisfaction and refine quantities as demand patterns change.
column12: Reduction in food waste per cover attributable to portion-size and preparation adjustments
column13: Lisbon Marriott Hotel: After using food-waste data to change preparation and presentation, the hotel reduced food waste as a percentage of sales by 50% in nine months, generating approximately €31,000 annualised food-cost savings, avoiding 16.9 tonnes CO2e and saving the equivalent of 10,000 meals per year.
column15: €31,000 annualised food-cost saving in the Lisbon Marriott case. Savings are site-specific and should not be treated as a universal hospitality benchmark.
column16: 16.9 tCO2e avoided annually in the Lisbon Marriott case. This is a case-specific result rather than a generic abatement factor.
column17: Lisbon Marriott achieved its 50% reduction within nine months. The case does not publish a formal payback period, but the annualised €31k saving demonstrates measurable operating benefit.
column18: Food waste g/cover; food waste as % sales; kg food avoided; £/€ food cost avoided; meals saved; tCO₂e avoided.
